childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_intro_image_alt: Parent holding and looking at a newborn baby
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_intro_paragraph_1: When babies are born their vision is poor. They are essentially 'blind'. Their vision will however develop over the following 5 to 8 years with most improvement occurring in the first 18 months of life. This is a very critical period.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_intro_paragraph_2: During this time the visual system of the eyes and brain needs to be healthy and stimulated. This is the best period to identify disease and refer for treatment.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_brain_image_alt: The eyes and their visual connections to the brain
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_identify_disease_titl: Why and how we identify disease to maximise visual development
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_identify_disease_body: Any disease of the eye or brain will slow development and limit long term vision. This is why it is important to identify as early as possible any treatable causes of disease that is affecting normal visual and general development.
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_question_bubble: This can be done by asking questions about vision, pregnancy, birth, any illnesses and general development
childhoodeyebrainimages.visual_development_observe_copy: then observe the eyes assessing visual development then screen for eye disease by performing the fundal 'red' reflex test and examining the front of the eye
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_1_paragr: Inside the womb, the unborn baby is surrounded by gentle and calming sound, including their mother's heartbeat and voices and sounds from the world outside.
As pregnancy reaches its final stages, the baby's eyes can open inside the womb.
While they can't yet see images or details, they can sense changes in light.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_1_image_: Pregnancy stage illustration of the unborn baby in the womb
Late pregnancy stage illustration showing awareness of light
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_2_paragr: At birth vision is very unlike that of an adult. A newborn is 'blind' with poor visual acuity of around 6/600. They do not perceive much colour and have low contrast sensitivity. They have no stereovision and their eyes may squint now and again.

They will however look directly at faces at very close range, and squeeze their eyes shut to bright lights. Their vision from now is going to develop very rapidly and become like an adult by 8 years of age.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_3_paragr: Within two weeks vision has improved hugely. They can now see some detail, especially if things are up close. There is no colour and what they do see is flat, because their eyes are not yet always straight and working together for depth perception.
Sometimes their eyes will drift in or out for a short while. This is called squinting. This should stop happening by three months.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_4_paragr: By one month colour vision is starting to develop. They will be much more visually interested especially to faces. They will also start to try to follow things that are moving.
They will become more and more aware of familiar sounds including well known voices like their family. And start to join up what they hear with what they see.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_4_image_: Visual development between two weeks and one month
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_5_paragr: By three months their eyes should always be straight and working together to create 3D vision. This new depth perception helps them reach for things more accurately. They will be able to follow things that are moving faster but it is hard to switch fixation from one face or object to another quickly.
They like to look at only one thing at a time. They may also start to make their first meaningful sounds.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_5_image_: Visual development between one and three months
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_6_paragr: An infant with normally developing vision will become excited at seeing a drinking cup or spoon and can routinely fix and follow a face at a distance of 1-2 metres as well as be able to differentiate between familiar and unfamiliar faces by both their faces and voices.
They can also start to see things that are further away. Driven by curiosity, they will begin to reach for things.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_7_paragr: At 6 to 12 months of age the visual acuity is improving and is around 6/36. The distance at which faces are looked at and recognised has extended to 2 metres. All elements of vision are improving with more accurate reach and grasp.

At this age they are becoming more interested in images in books and on television, although real objects are more engaging encouraging them to crawl and around their first birthday, walk towards objects of interest. Their babblings are developing, and sounds will become first words at this age as well.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_8_paragr: By 18 months, vision is quite adult like although still a bit blurry at visual acuity of around 6/18. They will now be able to recognise their name and be using more and more words.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_8_image_: Visual development between twelve and eighteen months
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_9_paragr: After 18 months of age vision still needs several years to mature. Normal adult visual acuity will be formed by the age of 8.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_9_image_: Visual development between eighteen months and eight years
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_10_parag: After the age of 8 the visual system may not improve well to treatment such as cataract surgery. Identification of disease and referral for treatment is therefore best done as early in life as possible.

It can be seen that a huge amount of development occurs between birth and 18 months of age and continues more slowly throughout the rest of childhood. During this period it is essential that the child is healthy with a disease free visual system and provided with a stimulating and educationally nourishing environment.
Early identification of disease with referral for treatment is important to help maximise both visual and general development.
childhoodeyebrainimages.normal_visual_development_stage_10_image: After eight years visual development illustration

videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_003: When dispensing eyeglasses it is important to exclude other underlying eye disease.

videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_005: glasses and what type and who may need referral for other diseases such as cataracts and
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_007: Start with distance visual acuity testing one eye at a time unaided and if reduced use a pinhole.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_008: then test near vision with both eyes together.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_009: There are typically five possible outcomes.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_010: If the distance in near visual acuity are both good,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_011: the patient does not need glasses.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_012: If the distance vision is reduced,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_013: but improves with the pinhole and the near vision is okay,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_014: then the patient is most slightly short-sighted, also known as myopic.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_015: If the distance vision is reduced but improves with the pinhole,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_016: and the near vision is also reduced,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_017: then the patient is most likely a long sighted,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_019: If the distance vision is okay,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_020: but the near vision is reduced,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_021: and the patient is over 40 years of age,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_022: then they have pressed biopia and need reading glasses.
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_023: Finally, if visual acuity is reduced
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_024: and does not improve with pinhole or glasses,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_025: then underlying eye disease is very likely,
videos_ure_arclight_eyeglasses_3dce0666.cue_026: patient needs examination with the arc light.

assessmentVisionPage.cue_001: This video describes how to prepare the child and mother or carer before performing the fundal red reflex tests in both newborns and older children.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_002: The child should be held securely yet comfortably, either on the lap, over a shoulder, or, if a baby, lying on their back.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_003: It is important for them to feel safe. Young babies can be restless and may need to be swaddled.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_004: Examining shortly after a feed can help as they will be relaxed and a little sleepy.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_005: Older children may settle by playing with a toy for a short while.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_006: Speak with a friendly tone and try to get down to their eye level.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_007: Explain what you are going to do and gain consent before you start.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_008: First, ask the mother or carer if they have seen anything wrong with their child's eye or vision and how long they have noticed the problem.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_009: Next, look at the child's face and eyes. Ask yourself some questions.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_010: Does the child seem to have pain in one or both eyes? Are the eyes open or are they keeping them tightly shut?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_011: Is there watering or discharge from the eyes? Are the eyes the same size? Are the eyelids swollen?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_012: Now, consider how the child is seeing. Move your face slowly from side to side, watching their eyes.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_013: Make some silent smiles. Does the child follow the movement of your face or respond to your silent smile?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_014: Again, ask yourself some questions. Do both eyes move freely and together?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_015: Are the eyes straight or is one eye turning inwards or outwards? Do the eyes wobble?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_016: You can also use the lights on the Arclight and picture targets to gain attention and assess the quality of vision.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_017: Move the target side to side, up and down. Look to see if the child is fixing and following the target.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_018: Can they reach and point accurately at the target?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_019: Often, only one eye cannot see well. You or the mother can cover one eye, then the other.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_020: Move the target and compare how the child behaves to when using both eyes, then one at a time.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_021: If the child does not like one eye being covered, it suggests the uncovered eye does not see so well.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_022: If you think you can see something wrong with the external eye, look more closely using the loupe end of the Arclight.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_023: Switch the lights on and move up close to around 6 cm. You may need to use your finger to gently open the eyelids.
assessmentVisionPage.cue_024: Ask yourself some questions. Is the white part of the eye pink or red? Is the pupil or cornea grey or white?
assessmentVisionPage.cue_025: Is the pupil round? Can you see any foreign bodies? Now you are ready to perform the reflex tests.

mumVisionPage.cue_001: Inside the womb, the unborn baby is surrounded by gentle and calming sounds, including their
mumVisionPage.cue_002: mother's heartbeat and digestive system and voices and sounds from the world outside. As
mumVisionPage.cue_003: pregnancy reaches its final stages, the baby's eyes can open inside the womb. While they can't
mumVisionPage.cue_004: yet see images or details, they can sense changes in light. So, while life in the womb is muffled
mumVisionPage.cue_005: and dim, it is far from silent. Birth is a huge change for a baby. They suddenly enter
mumVisionPage.cue_006: a world full of new, bright sights and loud sounds. Adjusting to this new world is a sensory
mumVisionPage.cue_007: awakening that kick-starts their development. In the first few weeks of life, the baby will
mumVisionPage.cue_008: startle and wake up if there are loud sounds. Their eyes are sensitive to bright lights,
mumVisionPage.cue_009: but they can still see very little. Their vision is, however, starting to develop at a staggering
mumVisionPage.cue_010: rate. Within two weeks, vision has improved hugely. They can now see some detail, especially
mumVisionPage.cue_011: if things are up close. There is no colour, and what they see is flat because their eyes
mumVisionPage.cue_012: are not yet always straight and working together for depth perception. Sometimes their eyes
mumVisionPage.cue_013: will drift in or out for a short while. This is called squinting. This should stop happening
mumVisionPage.cue_014: by three months. By one month, colour vision is starting to develop. They will be much
mumVisionPage.cue_015: more visually interested, especially to faces. They will also start to try to follow things
mumVisionPage.cue_016: that are moving. They will become more and more aware of familiar sounds, including well-known
mumVisionPage.cue_017: voices, like their family, and start to join up what they hear with what they
mumVisionPage.cue_018: see. By three months, their eyes should always be straight and working together to create
mumVisionPage.cue_019: 3D vision. This new depth perception helps them reach for things more accurately. They
mumVisionPage.cue_020: will be able to follow things that are moving faster. At the same time, meaningful sounds
mumVisionPage.cue_021: will start to be made. By six months, the baby should be able to recognise familiar people
mumVisionPage.cue_022: by both their faces and voices. They can also start to see things that are further
mumVisionPage.cue_023: away. Driven by curiosity, they will reach for things, crawl towards them, and, around
mumVisionPage.cue_024: their first birthday, walk. Their babblings are developing and sounds will become first
mumVisionPage.cue_025: words at this stage as well. By 18 months, vision is quite adult-like, although still
mumVisionPage.cue_026: a bit blurry. They will now be able to recognise their name and be using more and more words.
mumVisionPage.cue_027: Some babies may not achieve these developmental milestones at the expected time. There are
mumVisionPage.cue_028: many reasons for this, and many will correct themselves. For example, premature babies
mumVisionPage.cue_029: may have delays, but typically catch up later in childhood. For some, there may be persisting

usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_001: This video explains how to use the Arclight to perform the fundal red reflex by selecting the brightest light setting.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_002: Make sure the lens rack is at the top, where there is no lens power in the sight hole.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_003: At arm's length, observe the reflex in both eyes at the same time.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_004: Compare the brightness and colour between the two eyes.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_005: In a normal examination, there should be no overall difference in the brightness and colour between the two eyes.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_006: In white and Asian babies, the reflex can look more orange and yellow.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_007: These appearances are still all normal as the overall colour and brightness are the same between the two eyes.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_008: An abnormal reflex is when there is a persistent, real difference in the brightness and colour between the two eyes.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_009: This may be a displaced corneal reflection, a dark patch present within the reflex of one eye or both eyes, or a completely absent red reflex.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_010: An abnormal reflex test can indicate the presence of cataract, retinoblastoma, corneal scar, squint, or refractive error.
usaidFundalReflexExamPage.cue_011: These all require further assessment by a specialist.

usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_001: This video describes normal and abnormal fundal red reflex appearance.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_002: A normal fundal red reflex examination is when there is no overall difference in the brightness and colour between the two eyes with the central corneal reflections.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_003: Even a normal appearance of the fundal reflex will, however, vary depending on how far away you are and where the child is looking.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_004: It is an active dynamic examination where you should move side to side and back and forth in and around arm's length from the patient.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_005: Babies and children will also move their hands and eyes, making the reflex change the way it looks during the examination.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_006: In a black baby, the reflex typically looks quite pale, with yellow and white and sometimes even blue as the main colour.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_007: Importantly, in a normal examination, there should be no overall difference in the brightness and colour between the two eyes with the central corneal reflections.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_008: An abnormal reflex is when there is a persistent, real difference in the brightness and colour between the two eyes.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_009: A displaced corneal reflection, a dark patch present within the reflex of one eye or both eyes, or a completely absent red reflex.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_010: An abnormal reflex test can indicate the presence of cataract, retinoblastoma, corneal scar, squint, refractive error or congenital problems such as coloboma.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_011: These all require further assessment by a specialist.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_012: Look at this reflex and ask yourself: is this normal or abnormal? The answers will follow afterwards.
usaidNormalAbnormalPage.cue_013: You should now have a better understanding of what a normal reflex looks like, as well as abnormal reflexes, and be able to suggest the most likely cause.

questions.prompt: The vision of a patient has been recorded as 6/60 in their right eye. What was the most likely distance between the patient and the chart when their vision was tested?
questions.explanation: Snellen acuity is recorded as distance tested / line seen. Therefore, 6/60 means the patient was tested at 6 metres from the chart and saw line 60, typically the largest letter at the top of the chart.

questions.prompt: A patient was found to have visual acuity unaided of 6/24 but when tested with a pinhole it improved to 6/9. What is the most likely reason for this?
questions.explanation: If visual acuity improves when looking through a pinhole, the most likely reason is a refractive error such as myopia. Narrow parallel rays of light entering the eye are much less affected by refractive surfaces, so they pass through to the retina still in focus.

questions.prompt: When testing vision the patient could not see the biggest letter on the top line. What is the next step in testing their vision?
options: Try counting fingers or hand movements
Move the chart closer to the patient
Ask the patient to look through a pinhole
questions.explanation: If the patient cannot see the largest letter on the top line, halve the testing distance and see whether this allows them to see any letters. For example, if they cannot see line 60 at 6 metres, move to 3 metres. If they can then see the top line, record the visual acuity as 3/60.

questions.prompt: A patient read line ‘6’ on a chart when tested at 3 metres. Which visual acuity below records this most accurately?
questions.explanation: This patient has visual acuity of 3/6 (distance tested / line seen). The equivalent visual acuity would be 6/12, which is the same ratio and so is the most accurate.

questions.prompt: A patient’s visual acuity was recorded as NPL in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. What sight impairment category would they meet?
questions.explanation: Sight impairment categories are based on binocular vision. Even if someone is ‘blind’ in one eye, if they have normal vision in the other eye they are categorised as having normal vision.

questions.prompt: What is the technique used to test for an RAPD?
questions.explanation: There are three ways to test the pupil light response: direct, by viewing the pupil on which the light is shining; indirect or consensual, by observing the fellow pupil; and the swinging light test, by observing the pupil as the light arrives to look for an RAPD.

RAPD is tested using the swinging light test. This lets the examiner compare the afferent systems of both eyes while examining one eye, making it a relative way to identify whether one afferent system is defective compared with the other.

questions.prompt: What is the clinical sign seen in an RAPD?
options: Poor constriction of the pupil when light is shone on it
Dilation of the pupil when light is shone on it
No constriction when the light is shone on it
Dilation of the pupil when light is shone on the other eye
questions.explanation: The pupil will typically constrict when light is shone on it. During the swinging light test, paradoxical dilation when the light reaches an eye indicates that an RAPD is present on that side.

questions.prompt: When we test for an RAPD what parts of the visual pathway are we assessing?
options: The occipital lobe (vision centre) of the brain
The visual pathways from the midbrain to the occipital lobe
The lens, retina and optic nerve
questions.explanation: The retina and optic nerve form the anterior parts of the afferent system, taking information from the eye to the midbrain to initiate the motor or efferent response that changes pupil size.
Any disease of the retina or optic nerve that affects its afferent function can lead to an RAPD, including a vascular event affecting the retina.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the main purpose of the fundal ‘red’ reflex test in a newborn baby?
options: Identify disease obstructing the visual axis
Assess the health of the optic nerve
questions.explanation: In a newborn, the main purpose is to identify disease blocking light from entering the eye. This can include disease of the cornea, lens, vitreous, retina or optic nerve.

questions.prompt: A 3-month-old infant has a bright fundal ‘red’ reflex in the left eye but a much duller reflex in the right eye. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange urgent referral to an eye specialist
Arrange routine referral to an eye specialist
questions.explanation: Any abnormality on this test requires urgent assessment by an eye specialist because serious disease, such as cataract or retinoblastoma, may be present.

questions.prompt: A 9-month-old baby born at 36 weeks’ gestation presents with poor visual development and absent fundal reflexes in both eyes. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
questions.explanation: Loss of the fundal reflex is caused by something blocking light entering the eye. Retinopathy of Prematurity can cause retinal detachment, but is more common in babies born before 34 weeks. Retinoblastoma can cause loss of the reflex but is very rare, occurring in around 1 in 15,000 births. Cataract is the most common cause in babies and infants, occurring in around 1 in every 1,000 to 2,000 births.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions in an adult is least likely to cause an abnormal fundal ‘red’ reflex?
questions.explanation: Occipital lobe stroke is least likely. Although it causes loss of vision, this results from brain damage rather than disease affecting the clarity of the ocular media.

questions.prompt: What structures, and in what order, does light pass through to illuminate the fundus and produce the fundal ‘red’ reflex?
questions.explanation: Light passes through the cornea, lens and vitreous to reach the retina, a clear membrane overlying the choroid of the fundus from which light is reflected. Disease of the cornea, lens, vitreous, retina or choroid can therefore cause an abnormal fundal reflex test.
